source.title_on_document: Timing Matters: How Using LLMs at Different Timings Influences Writers' Perceptions and Ideation Outcomes in AI-Assisted Ideation

supplement.where: Appendix A 'Supplementary Materials', pp. 15-16 of this PDF
supplement.holds: Figure 7 (similarity with LLM ideas computed with text-embedding-ada-002 embeddings instead of TF-IDF; figure only, significance star) and Table 4 (one example ideation log). No additional tables of statistics.

paper_design_summary: Sixty Prolific participants were randomly assigned (30 per arm) to use a GPT-4 ideation tool either from the start of a 20-minute task (C_before) or only after generating at least three ideas on their own (C_after). The task was to generate as many supporting ideas as possible for a health-related claim (two topics, counterbalanced). Scored on the output: number of distinct supporting ideas, TF-IDF cosine similarity of the participant's ideas to the LLM ideas the participant saw, and within-person idea diversity from ada-002 embeddings; perceptions (self-efficacy, autonomy, ownership, credit) were self-reported.

studies.label: Online experiment: LLM before vs after independent ideation (supporting ideas for health claims)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Timing of access to the GPT-4 ideation component: available from the start (C_before) or unlocked only after the participant saved at least three independent ideas (C_after). Writing topic was counterbalanced.
assignment.quote: We recruited a diverse group of 60 participants through Prolific. These individuals were randomly assigned into two conditions, with 30 participants per condition.
assignment.locator: p. 3, Section 3.2 Participants; also p. 3, Section 3.3 Procedure ('the participants were randomly assigned to two conditions'); p. 4, Figure 1 (N = 60; N = 30 per arm)

arms.name: C_after
arms.description: Participants first generated at least three distinct ideas without AI (about 10 minutes), then could open the GPT-4 component to supplement or expand their ideas (about 10 minutes).

arms.name: C_before
arms.description: GPT-4 ideation component visible and usable from the start of the 20-minute ideation task.

participants.exclusions: No exclusions reported. The abstract reports 'a controlled experiment with 60 participants' and the idea-quantity t-test has t(58), consistent with all 60 analyzed. Per-arm analyzed counts are not printed separately (30 per arm is given at assignment, p. 3 and Figure 1).
participants.who: Prolific workers aged 21 to 50 (M = 31.167, SD = 8.061); 26 female, 34 male; 67 percent with at least a bachelor's degree; paid 5.85 USD for about 30 minutes
participants.quote: In a controlled experiment with 60 participants, we found that using LLMs from the beginning reduced the number of original ideas

ai_tool.name_model: OpenAI GPT-4 API in a custom web prototype (Vue.js front end, Django back end, hosted on Heroku)
ai_tool.how_used: Participants typed prompts in a prompt box, could pick and edit three default templates (each asking for four supporting ideas within 50 words), and read AI-generated ideas in a side panel while writing their own ideas in separate input fields (pp. 3-5, Sections 3.4, 3.4.1, 3.4.2; Figure 2).

task.description: Generate as many supporting ideas (arguments) as possible for a health claim: 'Excessive daytime sleepiness increases the risk of developing certain health conditions' or 'Applying urine to a jellyfish sting not only fails to ease the pain but can even worsen the sting'. Ideas did not need to be factual. Preceded by a 5-minute practice task with the prototype.
task.duration: About 20 minutes of ideation (C_after: 10 min independent + 10 min with LLM; C_before: 20 min with LLM); about 30 minutes in total (p. 3, Section 3.3; p. 4, Figure 1)

outcomes.name: Quantity of supporting ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of distinct supporting ideas the participant submitted, whether generated independently or with LLM help; redundant or repetitive ideas not counted (p. 5, Section 3.5.2). Who judged distinctness is not stated. In C_after the count mixes ideas written before AI was unlocked and ideas written with AI available.

contrasts.reported: Student t-test: t(58) = -1.897, p = 0.063, d = -0.490 (paper calls it marginal). C_before M = 3.867, SD = 2.285; C_after M = 5.567, SD = 4.345; n = 30 per arm at assignment. SEM (Table 2): Quantity of Ideas on LLM Usage Timing 1.563, SE 0.905, z 1.727, p 0.084, 95% CI [0.120, 3.210], controlling for creative self-efficacy, autonomy, ownership.
contrasts.locator: p. 7, Section 4.1; p. 8, Figure 3(a); p. 11, Table 2

outcomes.name: Similarity between participant ideas and LLM-generated ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: TF-IDF vectors with cosine similarity between each participant idea and each LLM idea that participant received; per-participant score averages over the participant's ideas (p. 5, Section 3.5.3; p. 6, Table 1). Higher = more overlap with the LLM's ideas; the paper reads lower similarity as more original ideas (Table 3: 'lower originality reflected by the higher idea similarity'). Robustness variant: same pipeline with OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002 embeddings, figure only (p. 5, footnote 8; p. 15, Figure 7). Not a comparison across people.

contrasts.reported: Welch t-test: t(48.36) = 4.778, p = 0.006, d = 0.747. C_before M = 0.899, SD = 0.404; C_after M = 0.648, SD = 0.250; n = 30 per arm at assignment. SEM (Table 2): Similarity with Ideas from LLM on LLM Usage Timing -0.244, SE 0.091, z -2.678, p 0.007, 95% CI [-0.397, -0.064]. Embedding variant: significant at p < 0.05 (star only), Figure 7(b).
contrasts.locator: p. 7, Section 4.1; p. 8, Figure 3(b); p. 11, Table 2; p. 15, Figure 7

outcomes.name: Participant's idea diversity (within-person)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Each idea in one participant's set embedded with OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002; diversity = 1 - mean pairwise cosine similarity over the upper triangle of that participant's similarity matrix (p. 5, Section 3.5.4). Variety among one person's own ideas, so coded flexibility, not across-people diversity. Excluded from the SEM (p. 9, footnote 11).

contrasts.reported: Welch t-test: t(36.472) = 1.337, p = 0.189, d = 0.345. Arm means and SDs not printed; distributions in Figure 3(c) (p-value: 0.189, ns). Sign convention of t and d not stated.

company_involvement.description: Acknowledgments: research partially supported by NUS IT's Research Computing group (NUSREC-HPC-00001) and AWS. No author affiliation with an AI company; the AI tool is OpenAI GPT-4 accessed through the API.

eligibility.reason: Individuals were randomly assigned between two generative-AI configurations (GPT-4 from the start vs after independent ideation), an ai_design comparison with no no-AI arm (p. 3, Sections 3.2-3.3). 60 people randomized, 30 per arm, no exclusions reported (close to the 50 threshold). Outcomes are computed on the submitted ideas: idea count (fluency), TF-IDF similarity to the LLM's ideas (paper reads as originality), and within-person embedding diversity. Borderline point: the task is generating supporting arguments for given health claims, which fits ideation (many acceptable answers, 'as many supporting ideas as they could') but was not rated for creativity by people.

one_line_finding: With 60 Prolific participants (30 per arm), unlocking GPT-4 only after independent ideation (C_after) vs from the start (C_before) gave marginally more ideas (5.567 vs 3.867; t(58) = -1.897, p = 0.063, d = -0.490), lower similarity to the LLM's ideas (0.648 vs 0.899; p = 0.006, d = 0.747), and no difference in within-person idea diversity (p = 0.189) (p. 7, Section 4.1; p. 8, Figure 3).
open_questions: Similarity outcome: printed t(48.36) = 4.778 does not match p = 0.006; the printed arm means and SDs (0.899/0.404 vs 0.648/0.250, n = 30 each) and d = 0.747 point to a t near 2.9. The extraction phase should not rely on the printed t (p. 7, Section 4.1).

Does generating supporting arguments for a given health claim count as a creative or ideation task under the codebook? No human creativity rating; the creativity-relevant outcomes are fluency and similarity to the LLM's ideas.
Construct of the similarity-to-LLM outcome: coded 'other' (paper interprets it as originality); a reviewer could argue 'novelty'.
ai_available_when_produced coded 'mixed': in C_after, part of each participant's submitted ideas was produced before AI was unlocked; in C_before, all ideas were produced with AI available.
Per-arm analyzed counts are not printed; only 30 per arm at assignment and t(58) for the quantity test.
notes: Self-reported outcomes (creative self-efficacy, autonomy, ownership, self-credit, credit to LLM; Mann-Whitney tests, p. 7-9, Figure 5) and the pre/post self-efficacy comparison (Figure 4) are not listed because they are not scored on the output. Task completion time (C_before 575.033 s, SD 338.897; C_after 711.433 s, SD 330.966; p. 5, Section 3.5.1) is a process measure, not listed. SEM with bootstrap (1000 samples) in Table 2 (p. 11) and Figure 6 (p. 10). Analysis software JASP v0.18.3. Treatment arm set to C_after because the paper proposes delaying LLM use; C_before is the default configuration (AI available throughout). Paper's d signs: d = -0.490 for quantity (C_after higher) and d = 0.747 for similarity (C_before higher), so d appears to be C_before minus C_after.
